Photograph: Kevin Bell Jr./AP Idaho Shooting at In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Idaho leaves multiple people dead, police say Police chief says the shooter is among the dead in ‘very chaotic scene’ near busy shopping area in Twin Falls Associated Press Sat 1 Aug 2026 21.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho on Saturday afternoon left multiple people dead and others injured, police said. The shooter was among the dead, Twin Falls police chief Matthew Hicks said in a news conference. Police were still trying to determine the shooter’s identity and motive. “We believe the threat to the community is over,” Hicks said. He added that he did not yet know exactly how many were killed or wounded, and officials were still in the process of notifying next of kin. “It was a very chaotic scene.” Before the news conference, Twin Falls county commissioner Brent Reinke said Sheriff Jack Johnson had told him five people were hurt. Lane Koehn, 34, said he was at a stoplight near the In-N-Out when he saw a person with an AR-style rifle emerge from the drive-thru. A man with a pistol started firing at the shooter. He then saw someone in an In-N-Out uniform drag a person bleeding from a gunshot wound in her chest across the parking lot. The employee, Koehn and the man with the pistol stayed until paramedics arrived for her. “She was pretty bad off, but I don’t know. I hope she made it,” Koehn said. Koehn said he was told by police to evacuate because the shooting was still active. He also said the shooter fired at least three or four rounds and it was not clear whether or not anyone in particular was targeted. The shooting took place near a busy shopping area and hundreds of people were there at the time, Hicks said. Police were interviewing witnesses and asked for anyone with information to contact authorities. Reinke, who is also former prison chief for the Idaho Department of Corrections, said he learned of the incident just before 4pm and multiple agencies responded. Police advised people to avoid the area as they closed roads. St Luke’s Magic Valley spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that the medical centre was “working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation”. Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 130 miles (205km) south-east of Boise and about 75 miles (120km) north of the Nevada border. https://www.empireofthekop.com/2026/08/1.text: (Photo by Naomi Baker/Getty Images) Liverpool have confirmed a new long-term contract for one defender who’s gone out on loan for this season. Calum Scanlon had been earmarked for another temporary spell at Cardiff City, to whom he was loaned out for the second half of last term, making eight appearances as they sealed an immediate return to the Championship. The left-back featured in all three of the Reds’ friendlies on their pre-season tour to the United States but wasn’t involved in the defeat to Monaco at Anfield last weekend ( Sofascore ). Scanlon signs new Liverpool deal and joins Cardiff on loan At midday on Saturday, Liverpool announced on their official website that the 21-year-old has signed a new long-term deal with the Reds and rejoined Cardiff on loan for the 2026/27 campaign. Scanlon could make the first appearance of his second spell for the Bluebirds on Monday night when they host Welsh rivals Wrexham in their first Championship fixture of the season. The left-back has made two competitive senior appearances for his parent club, both of which came in the Europa League group stage three years ago ( Transfermarkt ). Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust It seems a perfect outcome for Scanlon This appears to be the perfect outcome for the Birmingham native, who should (hopefully) enjoy regular game-time at a club with which he’s already familiar, whilst also being demonstrably shown plenty of faith by Liverpool in the form of his new contract. Barring an injury crisis at left-back (not wholly unthinkable at Anfield, in truth), Scanlon would’ve been left biding his time behind Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas had he remained on Merseyside, so he’s much better off to be out on loan and having a plausible chance of playing regularly this season. The Greece international’s contract expires next summer and it’s plausible that he could then leave the Reds, so there might be an opening for the Cardiff loanee to return to L4 at that stage as the foremost deputy for the Hungarian. He’ll be hoping to emulate Conor Bradley in using a successful EFL loan spell (Bolton, in the right-back’s case) as a springboard towards being ready for the Liverpool first team, with the Northern Ireland skipper capably backing up Trent Alexander-Arnold before then becoming a frequent starter under Arne Slot. We wish Scanlon the very best of luck in the Welsh capital and hope that he can avoid any recurrence of the injury troubles which haunted him over the past couple of years. https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: Web of intrigue … In the Shadows of Nuremberg View image in fullscreen Web of intrigue … In the Shadows of Nuremberg Movies Review In the Shadows of Nuremberg review – trial-adjacent thriller aims to be Russian answer to Saving Private Ryan A trivial personal plotline and a strain of maudlin patriotism undermine Nikolay Lebedev’s shaky telling of the Soviet side of the story Phil Hoad Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T aking place in the wings of the Nuremberg trial, this Soviet-side political thriller, first released back in 2023, features a scene in which the crowd turns on a boa-draped Hollywood floozy in town to entertain the troops. A case of mea culpa for director Nikolay Lebedev, who trivialises the momentous issues emerging from the courtroom by dressing the legal stuff up with a tenuous and shakily handled plotline about a missing soldier, in an attempt to make his film the Russian answer to Saving Private Ryan . After his brother goes MIA in the vicinity of the soon-to-be-historic city, Red Army intelligence officer Igor Volgin (Sergey Kempo) wangles a post translating for the Soviet delegation. He’s approached by Lena (Lyubov Aksyonova), a Russian wastrel with a perfectly coiffed bob despite months of forced labour in a German munitions factory; she claims to have run into his sibling, an artist, in captivity. But she is also feeding information to Helmut (Wolfgang Cerny), a Nazi resistance diehard who believes Göring (Carsten Norgaard) and company should be accountable only to German courts. A serious film unveiling the Soviet perspective on the trial, to accompany the likes of last year’s Russell Crowe vehicle Nuremberg , would have been fascinating. But if Lebedev felt his thriller needed a compelling personal throughline, Volgin’s quest isn’t it; the manhunt is only tangentially tied into the Nazi network, via a connection to art connoisseur Helmut that is mostly there to enable platitudes about beauty transcending war. And the underground elements are erratically threaded through to the bigger judicial picture, with Helmut’s attempt to reach Göring by blackmailing a key witness seemingly forgotten about by the end. Despite his track record with Russian blockbusters, Lebedev struggles to find a confident foothold in this haphazard web of intrigue. His twitchy camerawork can’t sit still, as if preferring the epic vistas of blitzed cityscapes over his protagonist. Without being overtly propagandist (despite its Russian state backing), the film displays a strain of maudlin patriotism – insisting how the Soviets are disdainfully treated by the allies and slandered by the Nazis at the tribunal – at odds with the film’s message: that Nuremberg was a moment when universal human justice took precedence over national interests. Not a capital crime, but Lebedev is unconvincing taking the stand. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: 2:02 Israelis and Palestinians react as Eisenkot given mandate to form government – video Israel Gadi Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he strives to form government Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’ Guardian staff and agencies Sun 8 Nov 2026 12.53 EST Last modified on Sun 8 Nov 2026 19.50 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis. Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority. “We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps.” Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community. Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court. In the US, Israel’s closest ally, Democrats on Tuesday swept the midterm elections, with calls to rein in Israel after the devastation in Gaza and the unpopular Iran war, which Netanyahu launched with Donald Trump. Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.” He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister. “My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said. US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu Read more Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier. Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority. During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote. Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties. Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox. Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties , which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Supporters of Benjamin Netanyahu stretch out a large Likud party campaign banner reading ‘Right or Palestine’ in Tel Aviv on Saturday evening. Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal. Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result. Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement. These types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse. Donald Trump’s power is on the wane. What next for Russia, Israel – and the rest of us? | Simon Tisdall Read more Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right. He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government. He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing. Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah. After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else. If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.
